SLOOS overlay on the December 14, 2022 FOMC communication:

- Credit supply tightened broadly: Banks reported tighter standards for C&I loans (including foreign banks) and across CRE segments (construction/land development, nonfarm nonresidential, multifamily). Consumer credit also tightened, notably for credit cards; auto loan standards were generally unchanged. Approval thresholds shifted up—less likely to approve FICO 620/680, more likely at 720—indicating a narrower credit box.
- Credit demand softened: Weaker demand for C&I loans across large, middle-market, and small firms; weaker demand for credit cards and auto loans; overall consumer loan demand roughly unchanged. One offset: stronger demand for HELOCs.
- Drivers and risk assessment: Banks cited a weaker economic outlook as a key reason for tightening and flagged elevated recession risk; demand weakness was tied to customer needs and slower inventory/accounts receivable growth.

Implication for the FOMC read: The statement is hawkish (ongoing rate increases, balance-sheet runoff, higher administered rates). But the SLOOS shows a negative credit-supply impulse and softer loan demand already tightening financial conditions beyond policy rates, raising downside risks for growth and particularly for CRE and discretionary consumption. That tilts the overall tone more negative than a pure policy-torque read.

Net: still hawkish on policy, but with a more negative macro-financial backdrop once SLOOS is incorporated.
